strengths: Novel and interesting framing: adapting EigenTrust-style eigenvector reputation systems (PageRank/Eigenmorality) to aggregate subjective LLM judgments of value alignment, filling a real gap between existing LM ranking systems (LMArena, Prompt-to-Leaderboard, LitmusValues) as clearly positioned in Table 1.

Methodologically careful pipeline: Bradley-Terry-Davidson model with learned tie propensities, a reflection-based judge scaffold, transposed comparisons to handle order bias, bootstrapped confidence intervals, and power-law analysis of CI length vs. sample size (Appendix F).

Good empirical hygiene in robustness analysis: sensitivity to scenario distribution (Table 5), model population composition (Table 6), and an adversarial 'greenbeard' collusion experiment (Section 6.3) that probes a genuine vulnerability of peer-evaluation systems.

Interesting and honest findings: only 21% of score variance is explained by the model vs. 79% by the persona; EigenBench rankings invert model self-reports on conservatism; score stability under population changes is quantified.
Strong reproducibility support: full constitutions, personas, judge prompts, data-collection pseudocode, and hyperparameters provided in extensive appendices.
weaknesses: The central validity claim is unverified: EigenBench scores reflect a consensus of LLM judges, but the paper presents no external validation against human judgments (even a small human-labeled subset) or any independent measure of alignment. The disagreement with self-reported surveys (Section 5) is interesting but does not demonstrate that EigenBench measures alignment rather than shared judge biases/lexicons.

The core premise — that a model better aligned with C is also a better judge of alignment with C — is asserted, not tested, and is arguably circular: the scores may largely measure the extent to which models share the judges' interpretations of the constitution, particularly since scores are heavily prompt-driven (79% persona variance suggests judge identity dominates).

The method is demonstrably gameable: greenbeard scores 'increase rapidly with G,' and the reassuring claim rests on the observation that prompted greenbeards don't always obey instructions (footnote 9), which is not a principled defense against adversarial manipulation.

The identifiability argument in Appendix D is not convincing as stated: Zermelo's result gives uniqueness of BT scores under connectivity conditions, and the paper conflates 'unique maximum value' with 'unique maximizer'; the rewritten trust matrix expression in Appendix D.1 also appears to contain errors (e.g., exp(θilk) dropped in the denominator).

Evaluation populations are small (N=5 models, N=25 model-persona pairs, N=4 in the character-training test), constitutions are few (three invented + two real), and the variance decomposition is performed on only one constitution; the 'character training' application is only a feasibility check with 4 models and no fine-tuning intervention.

Scores are sensitive to scenario distribution (e.g., Claude 4 Sonnet drops ~70 Elo from r/Ask to OASST) and to population composition, which complicates the 'values-to-leaderboard' use case; the paper reports these sensitivities but does not resolve or bound them.

Known LLM-as-judge pathologies (position bias, self-preference, verbosity bias, shared training-distribution artifacts across commercial models) are only partially addressed via the scaffold and inconsistency remapping; residual ~20% inconsistency is handled by ad-hoc tie overwriting.

strengths: The idea of combining peer evaluation, a Bradley-Terry-Davidson model with judge-specific 'lenses', and EigenTrust aggregation to quantify subjective traits without ground-truth labels is creative and the pipeline is clearly described with extensive implementation detail (constitutions, prompts, data collection algorithm, judge scaffolding).

The paper includes several useful robustness analyses: scenario-distribution sensitivity, model-population sensitivity, order-bias/cycle-rate judge quality tests, bootstrap confidence intervals, and a greenbeard (collusion) adversarial probe, which shows awareness of the key failure modes of peer-rating systems.

The 'double-blind' design (evaluees unaware of criteria, judges unaware of evaluee identities) and the transposed-comparison inconsistency handling are thoughtful engineering choices that mitigate some obvious LLM-judge biases.
Writing and figure presentation are generally clear, and the related-work positioning against LMArena, Prompt-to-Leaderboard, and LitmusValues is helpful.
weaknesses: Central validity claim is unsupported: the premise that 'a model whose behavior aligns better with C is also a better judge of alignment with C' is asserted, never validated, and is arguably circular — scores are weighted by judges whose quality is itself defined by the same scores. There is no human evaluation whatsoever; even a small human-annotated subsample to sanity-check EigenBench scores against human judgment of the constitutions would be essential and is missing.

The paper's own headline finding undermines its purpose: 79% of variance in trust scores is explained by the prompted persona and only 21% by the underlying model. The authors spin this as evidence of 'meaningful dispositions,' but it suggests the method largely measures the prompt, not the model — precisely the confound the benchmark claims to separate.

LLM judges are well known to exhibit self-preference and stylistic biases; although judges are 'double-blind,' they may still recognize their own outputs or favor responses stylistically similar to their own. No analysis of self-recognition or self-preference bias is provided, which is a first-order concern when models judge each other.

Many empirical results are weak or over-interpreted: the confidence intervals in Figure 3 overlap heavily for most models, yet the paper implicitly supports ranking conclusions; Table 3's 'Claude wins on OpenAI's spec' claim rests on a population of only 4 models; the survey baseline (Section 5) is a weak, near-strawman comparison, and disagreement with it does not validate EigenBench.

The greenbeard experiment actually demonstrates the method's vulnerability: greenbeard scores 'increase rapidly with G,' and the paper concedes in a footnote that the adversarial prompt was weak and a stronger one could dominate the ranking. For a benchmark intended for leaderboards and character-training validation, showing the mechanism is defeatable with the obfuscation happening implicitly (models could discover this organically) is a serious unresolved limitation.

The methodological novelty is modest: EigenTrust (2003), Davidson ties (1970), and Bradley-Terry are all established; the low-rank extension is reasonable but the identifiability argument in Appendix D is informal (invoking Zermelo's proof for the plain BT model without a complete proof for the present model), and the choice of latent dimension is driven by small test-loss differences.

Significant confounds in the constitution experiments go unaddressed: constitutions were co-written with specific LMs, and the authors note (Appendix A) the possibility that a constitution-writing model gets an unfair boost — a textbook conflict of interest for the headline results, acknowledged but never quantified or resolved.

Limited discussion of the ethical/political implications: constitutions encode contested ideological positions (e.g., the 'less woke' conservatism criterion), and the paper offers no framework for how such subjective 'value leaderboards' should be interpreted, audited, or guarded against misuse.
No code or artifact release is mentioned, limiting reproducibility of a benchmark paper whose value depends on exact prompts, scaffolds, and aggregation code.

strengths: Novel and interesting framing: adapting EigenTrust-style eigenvector reputation systems (with a low-rank Bradley-Terry-Davidson layer) to measure subjective value alignment of LMs is a creative contribution, and the paper clearly positions itself against LMArena, Prompt-to-Leaderboard, and LitmusValues.

Technically careful pipeline: double-blind data collection, transposed comparisons to handle order bias, a reflection scaffold empirically validated to reduce cycle rates and order bias (Appendix E), bootstrap confidence intervals, an identifiability argument extending Zermelo's proof, and an embedding-dimension ablation (Appendix G).

Thoughtful robustness analyses: scenario-distribution transfer (Table 5), population-sensitivity (Table 6), and an adversarial 'greenbeard' experiment probing manipulation of the score — a rare and commendable self-critique.

Interesting empirical findings: the variance decomposition showing ~21% of score variance attributable to the LM vs ~79% to the persona, and the striking divergence between self-reported and revealed values (Table 4), which is a genuinely useful observation about model surveys.
Well-written and transparent: full constitutions, personas, prompts, and data-collection algorithms are included, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central premise — that models better aligned with C are better judges of alignment with C — is asserted, not validated. No experiment tests whether EigenBench scores correlate with any external ground truth (e.g., human expert judgments, or alignment measured by other established methods). Without this, the circularity of LMs judging LMs is a serious validity concern: scores may largely reflect shared judge biases, sycophancy, or stylistic preferences rather than 'alignment.'

The headline decomposition result (79% of variance from persona, 21% from LM) arguably undercuts the paper's own motivating claim of measuring stable model dispositions; the interpretation is somewhat apologetic, and no statistical significance or uncertainty is attached to this 0.21 estimate.
Small populations (N=5) with overlapping 95% CIs in Figure 3 make most pairwise ranking claims statistically fragile; the paper does not discuss which rank differences are significant.

Known confounds are acknowledged but unresolved: constitutions partly written by the very models being scored (Gemini helping write Universal Kindness and ranking first), and greenbeard models demonstrably inflating their scores, with the mitigation essentially deferred ('with a more forceful prompt...').

The comparison to model surveys (Section 5) uses only self-ratings, a weak baseline; comparing against human or third-party LLM evaluations on the same scenarios would substantially strengthen the empirical case.

Significance and scope are modest: the method is demonstrated on a handful of proprietary models and a few hand-crafted constitutions, with no released leaderboard, code, or cost analysis mentioned, limiting immediate impact and reproducibility in practice.

strengths: Novel and interesting framing: adapting EigenTrust/eigenmorality ideas to peer evaluation of LLM values is a creative combination (LLM-as-judge, low-rank Bradley-Terry-Davidson, eigenvector centrality) that addresses a real gap in measuring subjective traits with no ground truth.

Methodologically careful pipeline: order-bias correction via transposed comparisons, tie propensity modeling, a reflection-based judge scaffold with empirical judge-quality metrics (Table 8), an identifiability argument for the trust matrix (Appendix E), and held-out model selection for latent dimension.

Multiple, largely well-designed validation experiments: human-judge comparison (human-human vs. human-LM interjudge distances), ground-truth recovery on GPQA (Kendall-tau ≈ 0.77 with a quantified improbability under random rankings), and robustness analyses across scenario datasets, constitution rewordings, and population changes.
Adversarial robustness analysis (Greenbeard experiment) proactively probes a known failure mode of peer-evaluation systems, which is unusual and commendable.
Substantial scale and reproducibility: up to 37 models, ~140k comparisons, full prompt/constitution details, model IDs, and released code.
weaknesses: The core premise — that better-aligned models are better judges — is assumed rather than demonstrated; correlated biases among frontier models (shared training data, RLHF pipelines, similar value priors) could produce a confident but systematically skewed 'consensus,' and this threat is not analyzed.

The GPQA validation has a circularity concern: the model population was selected using an external leaderboard, and success largely reflects that judges' knowledge correlates with correct answers; this is only a loose analogue for truly subjective traits, and notable rank errors (e.g., Kimi K2: 3rd vs. 8th) are downplayed.

Human validation is thin: only 7 judges (including authors/volunteers), one constitution, ~3000 comparisons, and the headline result — that average human-LM distance (0.3130) matches average human-human distance (0.3133) — is a weak statistic that is easily satisfied by diffuse, noisy trust vectors and does not establish that EigenBench recovers a meaningful consensus.

Missing key baselines: no empirical comparison of the eigenvector aggregation against a uniform average of judge scores (the method's central design choice, motivated only theoretically), nor against a single strong fixed judge or majority vote; the added complexity of the BTD + EigenTrust stack is not shown to be necessary.

Score stability is imperfect: Table 3 shows sizable rank reversals across scenario datasets (Claude 4 Sonnet 1530→1460, GPT 4.1 1478→1403), Deep Ecology confidence intervals are very wide, and the paper does not discuss how many samples users need for trustworthy rankings.

Practical concerns are under-addressed: cost scales roughly O(N²) with model population, and the theoretical justification for preferring eigenvector over mean rests on an unvalidated assumption (acknowledged in footnote 4) whose validity varies by constitution.

Novelty is primarily combinational rather than conceptual — EigenTrust (2003), BTD (1970), and LLM-as-judge are all established; the contribution is their integration, and the paper would benefit from sharper theoretical analysis of when the fixed point t is well-conditioned or manipulable.

strengths: The paper tackles a genuinely interesting and underexplored problem: quantifying subjective traits of LMs for which no ground-truth labels exist, and the application of EigenTrust-style eigenvector aggregation to LM peer judgments is a creative synthesis of ideas from Eigenmorality, Bradley-Terry-Davidson models, and LLM-as-judge evaluation.

The experimental scope is extensive: model rankings across three constitutions, a 37-model large population run (~140k comparisons), persona vs. LM variance decomposition, sensitivity analyses over scenario distributions, constitution wording, and population composition, plus judge-quality tests (order bias, cycle rates) that validate the reflection scaffold.
The adversarial 'Greenbeard' experiment is a thoughtful stress test of the method's collusion vulnerability, and the authors honestly report that greenbeards can inflate their own scores.
The writing is generally clear, the pipeline is well documented (prompts, model IDs, algorithms in appendices), and code availability supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core premise is asserted rather than established: that models whose behavior better aligns with a constitution are also better judges of alignment (footnote 4 admits this likely fails for some traits). Because scores are the fixed point of exactly this assumption, the method risks circularity: the 'consensus judgment' may simply reflect the biases and shared idiosyncrasies of the judge population (e.g., correlated family/style biases among frontier models) rather than any meaningful notion of value alignment.

The human validation is too weak to support the central claim. It uses only 7 judges (including the authors, who share training and priors), a single constitution (Universal Kindness), ~3000 comparisons, and a weak metric: similarity between human-human and human-LM trust vectors. High mutual agreement among a small, non-representative judge pool does not establish that the scores track 'alignment' in any normatively meaningful sense; the paper itself frames these traits as subjective, which undercuts using agreement as validation.

A key ablation is missing: EigenTrust/eigenvector weighting is never empirically compared to the simple uniform average 1/N sum T_ij or to majority-vote aggregation of a single strong judge. Without this, the contribution reduces to a known pairwise-ranking pipeline (BT-D + LLM judges) with an unverified extra aggregation step.

The GPQA 'ground truth recovery' result conflates competence with judgment quality and lacks baselines: a ranking within tau~0.77 of ground truth (12 adjacent swaps among 15 models) is not particularly strong, and simpler baselines (e.g., each judge's own answers scored by majority agreement, or judge accuracy on the option-selection task) are not reported, so the headline 'one in two hundred thousand' framing overstates what is demonstrated.

The Greenbeard experiment shows the method is manipulable: adversarial models (or their developers) can inflate scores, and the authors concede a 'more forceful prompt' would let a majority of colluders dominate the leaderboard. For a proposed leaderboard/training-target application, this is a serious unsolved robustness problem, not a footnote.

Data handling choices are ad hoc and potentially distorting: overwriting order-inconsistent preferences with ties changes the data-generating process, ties dominate in some conditions (Deep Ecology), and ~20% inconsistent judgments are remapped rather than modeled.

Consequences and ethics of 'values-to-leaderboard' scoring are underexamined: ranking models on politically contested value systems (e.g., conservatism) with self-selected constitutions invites Goodharting and misuse (the paper cites Goodhart's law in its own motivation but does not confront it for its own metric), and using EigenBench scores as an RLHF/DPO-style optimization target would likely make the metric gamed rather than informative.

Significance is limited: several components (pairwise LLM judging, Elo/BT aggregation, position-bias controls) are standard practice; the novel element (eigenvector trust weighting) is the part with the least empirical support.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated method: adapting EigenTrust/eigenvector-based consensus to LLM peer evaluation of subjective traits is a creative contribution to a timely problem (measuring value alignment without ground truth labels), with clear positioning relative to LMArena, Prompt-to-Leaderboard, and LitmusValues.

Multi-pronged validation design: the paper validates from several independent angles—human agreement (Section 5.2), recovery of ground-truth rankings on GPQA without labels (Section 5.3, Kendall-tau ~0.77), validation of an external character-training pipeline (Table 2), and stated-vs-revealed value comparisons—rather than relying on a single metric.

Extensive robustness analysis: sensitivity to scenario distributions, constitution wording, and population composition (Section 6), judge-quality/scaffold ablations (Appendix J), embedding-dimension and sample-size stability analysis (Appendix K), and an adversarial 'Greenbeard' stress test (Appendix L) that proactively probes a known failure mode of trust/reputation systems.

Technical care: order-bias correction via transposed comparisons, reflection scaffold shown to reduce cycle and order bias, an identifiability argument for the trust matrix via Zermelo uniqueness (Appendix E.1), and principled bootstrap confidence intervals.

Practical relevance and reproducibility: direct application to character training (Constitutional AI-style pipelines), code release, and full prompt/constitution details in the appendix make the pipeline replicable.
weaknesses: The central premise—that models better aligned with C are better judges of alignment with C—is asserted rather than validated for subjective constitutions. The GPQA experiment tests it only for an objective task; for kindness/conservatism/ecology, the circularity concern (consensus reflects shared model biases, not genuine alignment) cannot be excluded, and the paper's abstract claims are stronger than this evidence warrants.

Human validation is thin and potentially biased: only seven judges (including the authors), one constitution (Universal Kindness), and one scenario source. The headline evidence that 'LM judges approximate human judgments as closely as humans approximate each other' rests on 1-norm distance similarity (0.3130 vs 0.3133), which shows comparable dispersion, not close agreement, and provides no rank-correlation or significance analysis.

Scores are ensemble-relative and demonstrably unstable under population changes: Table 4 shows Grok 4's score drifting ~23 Elo points and suspicious in-family effects (Claude 4 Sonnet's score rising when Claude 3.5 Haiku is added), yet possible same-family judging bias is never analyzed despite frontier labs contributing multiple models.

Known LLM-as-judge confounds are incompletely addressed: order bias is handled, but response-length/verbosity bias, stylistic similarity preferences, and self-preference are not measured, and many ranking differences in Figure 3 have overlapping bootstrap confidence intervals without statistical testing.

Adversarial robustness is only partially resolved: the Greenbeard experiment shows scores of adversarial models rise rapidly with their share of the population, and the authors concede a 'more forceful prompt' would let a majority dominate—leaving the method vulnerable to exactly the manipulation scenario it is meant to police.

Cost and scope limitations are acknowledged but not mitigated: five API calls per comparison, evaluation restricted to English, Western-centric constitutions and r/AskReddit-style scenarios, and rankings that provide relative rather than absolute calibration of alignment.

Novelty is moderate at the methodological level: EigenTrust (2003) and Bradley-Terry-Davidson are standard components combined here with a new application; related work on LLM judge ensembles and peer-prediction mechanisms could be more thoroughly integrated.
